claims.text: High configurational entropy kinetically hinders atomic diffusion in high-entropy nanoalloys at high temperatures.
High configurational entropy kinetically hinders elemental segregation at high temperatures.
The proposed kinetic hindrance prevents grain coarsening and phase separation.
The proposed kinetic hindrance improves resistance to oxidation.
High-entropy nanoalloys are more structurally and chemically stable at high temperatures than low-entropy analogues.
Multiple principal elements can be uniformly mixed to produce homogeneous, configurationally complex nanoalloys.
Disordered atomic packing is associated with sluggish diffusion at grain boundaries and within the lattice.
Sluggish grain-boundary and lattice diffusion impedes atomic migration and phase transitions.
High configurational entropy creates a rugged energy landscape.
A rugged energy landscape slows atomic mobility.
Reduced atomic mobility limits grain-boundary migration and elemental diffusion.
Limited grain-boundary migration and elemental diffusion reduce the rates of phase transformation, segregation, and oxidation.
Under identical high-temperature conditions, high-entropy nanoalloys will exhibit less grain growth than low-entropy analogues.
Under identical high-temperature conditions, high-entropy nanoalloys will exhibit less elemental segregation than low-entropy analogues.
Under identical high-temperature conditions, high-entropy nanoalloys will exhibit less oxidation than low-entropy analogues.
Low-entropy analogues have higher atomic mobility and less kinetic hindrance than high-entropy nanoalloys.
The prediction is intended to apply between 600 and 1000 degrees Celsius when diffusion and phase transformations are active.
At sufficiently low temperatures, atomic migration may be too limited for configurational-entropy effects on degradation to be distinguishable.
At sufficiently high temperatures, kinetic hindrance may be overcome.
Particle size, synthesis-related defects, sintering, and coalescence may alter diffusion rates or the predicted stability.
